title: Black Hole Seeds and Little Red Dots: Connecting Formation and Growth with a JWST Multi-Cycle Treasury Program
comment: Theory white paper on black hole seeds and Little Red Dots, submitted to the STScI call for JWST Multi-Cycle Treasury concept white papers as part of the Genesis Initiative (www.jwst-genesis.com). 5 pages (plus affiliations and references)
summary: JWST has revealed an abundant population of faint active galactic nuclei and a new class of compact, high-redshift sources known as Little Red Dots (LRDs), whose physical nature remains debated, with accreting massive black holes among the leading explanations. The emerging demographics of early black holes, with their high inferred number densities and, in some systems, the apparent excess of black hole mass relative to stellar mass, challenge simple scenarios of black hole seeding and growth. Despite these observational breakthroughs, the origin of early massive black holes remains uncertain, because "black holes have no memory": current samples cannot separate the imprint of seeding from subsequent growth. This white paper identifies the multi-cycle JWST observations needed to revolutionize our understanding of early black hole growth by: (i) distinguishing seeding pathways, (ii) constraining early black hole growth mechanisms, (iii) resolving the physical nature of broad-line emitters and LRDs, and (iv) testing black hole-galaxy co-evolution. These tasks require uniformly selected samples extending to low black hole and host-galaxy masses, allowing self-consistent measurements of black hole mass functions, Eddington-ratio distributions, and host properties. Grating spectroscopy, deep MIRI imaging, and variability analysis through repeated observations of the same fields would provide complementary tests of black hole formation and growth, their connection to host-galaxy evolution, and the nature of newly discovered populations of LRDs. In this white paper, we argue that these joint tests require a coordinated JWST Multi-Cycle Treasury program; such a program could provide the depth, uniformity, and time baseline needed to place substantially stronger, complementary constraints on early black hole formation, growth, and their connection to galaxy evolution.

AI.tldr: A white paper arguing that a coordinated JWST Multi-Cycle Treasury program—combining grating spectroscopy, deep MIRI imaging, and repeated-field variability observations—is needed to disentangle early black hole seeding from growth, characterize Little Red Dots and broad-line emitters, and test black hole–galaxy co-evolution at high redshift.
AI.motivation: JWST has uncovered abundant faint AGN and compact high-z Little Red Dots, with high inferred number densities and possible black hole mass excess over stellar mass challenging simple seeding/growth scenarios. Because "black holes have no memory," current samples cannot separate the imprint of seeding from subsequent growth, leaving the origin of early massive black holes uncertain.
AI.method: Proposes a coordinated JWST Multi-Cycle Treasury program with uniformly selected samples extending to low black hole and host-galaxy masses, enabling self-consistent black hole mass functions, Eddington-ratio distributions, and host properties. Complementary techniques: grating spectroscopy, deep MIRI imaging, and variability analysis via repeated observations of the same fields.
AI.result: The abstract presents a programmatic case rather than new measurements: the proposed joint tests would address (i) distinguishing seeding pathways, (ii) constraining early growth mechanisms, (iii) resolving the physical nature of broad-line emitters and LRDs, and (iv) testing black hole–galaxy co-evolution.
AI.conclusion: A coordinated JWST Multi-Cycle Treasury program could deliver the depth, uniformity, and time baseline required to place substantially stronger, complementary constraints on early black hole formation, growth, and their connection to galaxy evolution.

title: The obscured nucleus of NGC3256 S. I. Anisotropic AGN near-IR radiation field traced by CO v=1-0 with JWST/NIRSpec
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A. 9 pages, 5 figures
summary: The southern nucleus of NGC3256, a nearby luminous infrared (IR) interacting system (d=40 Mpc; L(IR)=10^11.6 Lsun), hosts a deeply obscured low-luminosity active galactic nucleus (AGN) associated with a massive and fast bipolar collimated molecular outflow. JWST/NIRSpec observations revealed bright spatially resolved ro-vibrational CO v=1-0 4.67um emission at the base of this molecular outflow extending out to ~300pc, which is excited by the ~4.7um IR radiation from the southern dusty core. Using Monte Carlo radiative transfer (MCRT) models, we analyzed the CO v=1-0 band emission to determine the intensity of the ~4.7um IR radiation field across the outflow base. We find that the core spectral luminosity density at ~4.7um, as seen by the material in the outflow base, is ~2-4 times higher than that inferred along our line of sight, indicating an anisotropic near-IR radiation field. Moreover, the slower than d^-2 decrease of the near-IR flux density across the outflow base suggests a collimated radiation field, for which we estimate a small half-opening angle (15-20deg) and a diameter of the collimating structure of 15 +- 5 pc. This is slightly smaller than the diameter of the obscuring envelope (25 +- 5 pc). Combined with the expansion of this obscuring envelope, traced by the blueshifted CO v=1-0 absorption toward the nucleus, this suggests that the AGN is beginning to clear its environment. We estimate N_H~10^22-23 cm^-2 for NGC 3256 S, which is similar to that of Type 2 AGN. However, in contrast to Type 2 AGN, a high covering factor of the obscuring material, possibly sustained by inflows linked to the galaxy merger, and similar to that expected in deeply obscured compact obscured nuclei (CONs), is needed to explain the absence of extended high-ionization emission. Therefore, NGC 3256 S shares properties with CONs and Type 2 AGN.

AI.tldr: JWST/NIRSpec observations of bright ro-vibrational CO v=1-0 emission at the base of a massive molecular outflow in NGC 3256 S reveal an anisotropic, collimated near-IR radiation field from a deeply obscured low-luminosity AGN that appears to be clearing its environment.
AI.motivation: The southern nucleus of NGC 3256 hosts a deeply obscured low-luminosity AGN driving a fast bipolar molecular outflow, but the geometry and intensity of the near-IR radiation field illuminating the outflow base, and the nature of the obscuration, remain poorly constrained.
AI.method: Monte Carlo radiative transfer (MCRT) modeling of the spatially resolved CO v=1-0 4.67um band emission observed with JWST/NIRSpec out to ~300 pc from the nucleus, used to infer the ~4.7um radiation field intensity, its radial profile, collimation, and the AGN column density.
AI.result: The core spectral luminosity density at ~4.7um seen by the outflow-base material is ~2-4 times higher than along the line of sight, indicating anisotropy. The flux declines more slowly than d^-2, implying a collimated field with half-opening angle 15-20 deg and collimating-structure diameter 15 +/- 5 pc, slightly smaller than the obscuring envelope (25 +/- 5 pc). Estimated N_H ~ 10^22-23 cm^-2, similar to Type 2 AGN, but a high covering factor of obscuring material is required to explain the absence of extended high-ionization emission.
AI.conclusion: NGC 3256 S shows a collimated, anisotropic near-IR radiation field and an AGN beginning to clear its obscuring envelope via expansion; it shares properties of both compact obscured nuclei (CONs) and Type 2 AGN.

title: AGN Archaeology: A Systematic Search for Fading AGN in MaNGA
comment: 22 pages, 9 figures (+2 appendix figures), 2 tables. Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal
summary: Active galactic nuclei (AGN) vary on broad timescales, but are primarily thought to "flicker" on and off during episodes of high and low accretion. Supermassive black holes (SMBHs) which are actively accreting material often show optical spectra dominated by AGN emission in their nuclei and beyond. In this work we develop an empirical model to quantify the fractional AGN contribution to optical spectra using the Baldwin-Phillips-Terlevich (BPT) emission line diagnostic diagram. We leverage this model against integral field unit (IFU) data from the Mapping Nearby Galaxies at Apache Point Observatory (MaNGA) survey to select 34 galaxies with weak nuclear AGN activity relative to their AGN signatures at large radii; this signifies past AGN activity which is fading with time (i.e., fading-AGN). The majority of our fading-AGN reside in edge-on systems undergoing minor mergers. We construct a simple model consisting of a disk galaxy with ionization cones and find that the orientation of such a system will impact its BPT classification in both single-fiber and IFU observations. The mean distance to the extended AGN emission in our sample corresponds to a light-travel time of $1.1\times10^4$ years. We use this to set a lower-limit on the typical lifetime of the AGN phase ($t_{\text{AGN}}>1.3\times10^5$ years) which is consistent with SMBHs growing via brief accretion bursts. These fading-AGN allow us to probe the elusive period of post-AGN galaxy evolution, and they give a $\sim10^4$ year baseline for understanding the accretion history in these systems.

AI.tldr: The paper builds an empirical BPT-based model to quantify fractional AGN contribution to optical spectra, applies it to MaNGA IFU data to identify 34 "fading-AGN" galaxies with weak nuclear but strong extended AGN signatures, and uses the extended emission scale to place a lower limit on the AGN lifetime.
AI.motivation: AGN are thought to flicker between high- and low-accretion episodes, but the post-AGN/fading phase of galaxy evolution is poorly probed. The authors aim to identify and characterize systems whose AGN activity is declining with time, and to constrain the typical duration of the AGN phase.
AI.method: An empirical model is developed to quantify the fractional AGN contribution to optical spectra using the BPT emission-line diagnostic diagram. This model is applied to MaNGA IFU data to select galaxies with weak nuclear AGN activity relative to AGN signatures at large radii. A simple disk-galaxy-plus-ionization-cones model is constructed to assess how system orientation affects BPT classification in both single-fiber and IFU observations.
AI.result: 34 fading-AGN galaxies are selected, most residing in edge-on systems undergoing minor mergers. Orientation is shown to affect BPT classification in both single-fiber and IFU data. The mean distance to extended AGN emission corresponds to a light-travel time of 1.1×10^4 years, yielding a lower limit on the AGN phase lifetime of t_AGN > 1.3×10^5 years.
AI.conclusion: The derived lifetime lower limit is consistent with SMBHs growing via brief accretion bursts. Fading-AGN provide a means to probe the elusive post-AGN phase of galaxy evolution and offer a ~10^4-year baseline for studying accretion history in these systems.

title: Phase Offsets Between the Minimum Light and Radial Velocity in Long Secondary Period Stars
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures, 1 table, submitted to ApJ
summary: Long secondary periods (LSPs), observed in a substantial fraction of luminous red giants, remain one of the longstanding problems in red giant variability. Previous studies have found a systematic phase relation between their photometric and radial velocity (RV) variations. We investigate this relation using ASAS-SN photometry and Gaia RV curves for 983 LSP stars, and compare it with other types of Long Period Variables. We confirm that LSP stars have a relatively narrow distribution of phase offsets between the phase of minimum RV and minimum light, with a mean value of $Δφ=-0.15\pm0.10$ in phase ($-0.96\pm0.64$ rad). Interestingly, this phase offset is similar for Miras, showing that this quantity is not sufficient to distinguish LSPs from pulsational variability. However, pulsating red giants show a relation between period and RV amplitude, with the RV amplitude generally increasing toward longer periods. LSP stars deviate from this relation, showing RV amplitudes of only a few km/s despite their long periods. The stacked light and RV curves of the LSP sample also show remarkable homogeneity and a coherent phase relation. In the binary interpretation of LSPs, the observed phase offset requires the obscuring material to be shifted in orbital phase with respect to the companion, consistent with models in which a low-mass companion produces a dusty wake in the wind of the red giant.

AI.tldr: Using ASAS-SN photometry and Gaia radial velocities for 983 long secondary period (LSP) stars, the authors confirm a narrow phase offset between minimum RV and minimum light, show it is shared with Miras and thus not diagnostic, but find that LSPs deviate from the period–RV amplitude relation of pulsating red giants, supporting a binary/dusty-wake interpretation.
AI.motivation: LSPs occur in a large fraction of luminous red giants yet remain unexplained. A previously reported systematic phase relation between photometric and RV variations could help discriminate between pulsation and binary scenarios, so a large, homogeneous sample is needed to characterize it.
AI.method: Cross-matched ASAS-SN light curves with Gaia RV curves for 983 LSP stars, measuring the phase offset between minimum RV and minimum light. Compared the offset with other long-period variables (notably Miras) and examined the period–RV amplitude relation, including stacked light and RV curves of the LSP sample.
AI.result: LSP phase offsets are narrowly distributed with mean Δφ = −0.15 ± 0.10 in phase (−0.96 ± 0.64 rad). Miras show a similar offset, so this quantity alone cannot separate LSPs from pulsation. Pulsating red giants follow a period–RV amplitude relation with amplitude growing toward longer periods, while LSPs deviate, displaying amplitudes of only a few km/s at long periods. Stacked curves reveal high homogeneity and a coherent phase relation.
AI.conclusion: The phase offset is not sufficient to distinguish LSPs, but the RV amplitude anomaly and the coherent stacked signal support a binary origin. The observed offset requires obscuring material to be shifted in orbital phase relative to the companion, consistent with a low-mass companion producing a dusty wake in the red giant's wind.

title: A multi-epoch VLBI study of compact symmetric objects as contaminants in the search for milli-lenses
comment: 25 pages, 12 figures, submitted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: The Lambda Cold Dark Matter model predicts a high abundance of low-mass dark matter halos, which can be probed through milliarcsecond-scale gravitational lensing (milli-lensing) of background radio-loud active galactic nuclei (AGNs). The Search for MIlli-LEnses (SMILE) project aims to find these rare systems with Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI). However, compact symmetric objects (CSOs) can closely resemble milli-lenses in VLBI images and are the main contaminant in such searches. We aim to determine the nature of the nine remaining milli-lens candidates of the SMILE pilot study and to characterize their physical properties. We analyzed all available multi-epoch, multi-frequency archival VLBI data, new HSA and EVN observations, and single-dish and connected-element interferometer measurements. We tested the lensing hypothesis through the morphology and spectra of the sources, and characterized their kinematics, spatially resolved spectral indices, magnetic fields, and integrated spectra, using synchrotron self-absorption (SSA) and free-free absorption (FFA) models. We identify eight of the nine candidates as CSOs, four of them for the first time. Spectral index asymmetries between components and previously undetected emission connecting them rule out the lensing hypothesis. Only J0923-3435 remains ambiguous. For the CSOs with known redshifts, the lobes have equipartition magnetic fields of $\sim$20-320 mG and projected separations of $\sim$60-240 pc, and show no measurable expansion, implying kinematic ages of at least $\sim$50-950 yr. The integrated spectra of J0210-2213 and J2347-1856 favor an inhomogeneous external free-free absorber over homogeneous and inhomogeneous SSA models. Since CSOs will be the main contaminant in the full SMILE survey, applying this framework will provide the same constraints for a much larger sample of compact radio-loud AGNs.

AI.tldr: Analysis of the nine remaining SMILE milli-lens candidates shows eight are compact symmetric objects (not lenses), with one (J0923-3435) still ambiguous; the CSOs are compact, magnetically dominated, and kinematically old, and external free-free absorption is favored for two sources.
AI.motivation: In LCDM, low-mass halos are abundant and can be probed via milliarcsecond gravitational lensing of radio-loud AGNs, but compact symmetric objects mimic milli-lens morphologies in VLBI images and are the dominant contaminant, so candidate nature must be resolved before lensing searches can proceed.
AI.method: Analysis of multi-epoch, multi-frequency archival VLBI data plus new HSA and EVN observations and single-dish/connected-element interferometry; lensing tested via morphology and spectra; kinematics, spatially resolved spectral indices, magnetic fields, and integrated spectra modeled with synchrotron self-absorption and free-free absorption.
AI.result: Eight of nine candidates identified as CSOs (four new); spectral index asymmetries and previously undetected connecting emission rule out lensing; only J0923-3435 remains ambiguous. For CSOs with known redshifts, equipartition fields ~20-320 mG, projected separations ~60-240 pc, no measurable expansion implying kinematic ages of at least ~50-950 yr. J0210-2213 and J2347-1856 integrated spectra favor an inhomogeneous external free-free absorber over homogeneous and inhomogeneous SSA.
AI.conclusion: CSOs are the main contaminant for the full SMILE survey; the framework provides a scalable method to characterize and reject CSO contaminants and constrain compact radio-loud AGN properties in larger samples.

title: The Composition of M-dwarf Exoplanet Hosts: Atmospheric Parameters and O, Mg, Si, and Fe Abundances from IR Spectroscopy
comment: 23 pages, 11 figures, accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal
summary: Determining M-dwarf abundances is an important step to discerning the chemical evolution of the Milky Way and characterizing exoplanetary systems, especially since these objects commonly host small exoplanets. However, a dearth of M-dwarf abundance measurements exist compared to Sun-like stars, partially due to their complicated optical spectra dominated by molecular absorption lines and low luminosities. To overcome these issues, we have obtained high resolution H-band spectra of 40 planet-hosting M-dwarf stars and 2 M-dwarfs in wide binaries with FGK primaries with IGRINS on Gemini South and on the McDonald Observatory 2.7m telescope, and NIRSPEC on Keck. Abundances were derived by comparing each observed spectrum to synthetic spectral grids generated with MOOG and MARCS atmospheric models. Effective temperatures were derived using OH and H$_{2}$O lines and [Fe/H] from Fe I and FeH lines. Both Mg and Si abundances were determined using atomic features. Overall, we find that our abundances are broadly consistent with previous literature M-dwarf abundances. We complemented our abundances analysis with UVW velocities and Milky Way stellar population membership probabilities and identified 2 potential thick disk stars from our kinematic and chemical analysis: GJ 1252 and L181-1 which was a previously known thick disk star. Kinematic stellar population probabilities and a low [Fe/H] abundance makes Kepler 42 a likely thick disk star, although uncertain Mg and Si abundances make classification difficult. Lastly, we have determined Si/Mg and Fe/Mg molar ratios for M-dwarf exoplanet hosts and find the abundance distributions leads to exoplanet core-mass fractions between 20 - 40$\%$.

AI.tldr: High-resolution H-band spectra of 42 M-dwarfs yield abundances broadly consistent with literature; kinematic and chemical analysis identifies two potential thick-disk stars (GJ 1252, L181-1) and a likely one (Kepler 42), while Si/Mg and Fe/Mg ratios imply exoplanet core-mass fractions of 20–40%.
AI.motivation: M-dwarf abundances are key to understanding Milky Way chemical evolution and characterizing exoplanetary systems (M-dwarfs commonly host small planets), yet measurements are scarce relative to Sun-like stars because of molecular-dominated optical spectra and low luminosities.
AI.method: High-resolution H-band spectra of 40 planet-hosting M-dwarfs and 2 M-dwarfs in wide binaries with FGK primaries, obtained with IGRINS (Gemini South, McDonald 2.7m) and NIRSPEC (Keck). Abundances derived by matching observed spectra to synthetic grids from MOOG and MARCS models; Teff from OH and H2O lines, [Fe/H] from Fe I and FeH, Mg and Si from atomic features. Complemented with UVW velocities and Milky Way population membership probabilities.
AI.result: Abundances broadly consistent with prior literature M-dwarf values. Two potential thick-disk stars identified (GJ 1252 and L181-1, the latter previously known); Kepler 42 likely thick disk based on kinematic probabilities and low [Fe/H], though uncertain Mg/Si complicate classification. Si/Mg and Fe/Mg molar ratios for M-dwarf exoplanet hosts yield core-mass fractions of 20–40%.
AI.conclusion: Near-infrared H-band spectroscopy enables reliable M-dwarf abundance determination despite optical spectral challenges. Combining chemistry with kinematics supports thick-disk identification, and derived refractory element ratios translate into exoplanet core-mass fractions of 20–40%, informing interior composition of planets around M-dwarfs.

title: DOWSING, Dust Observations With SCUBA-2 In Nearby Galaxies: I. Dust in M81
comment: 18 pages, 21 figures. Accepted for publication in MNRAS on 2 November 2026
summary: We present a resolved far-infrared/sub-millimetre study of dust in the nearby spiral galaxy M81 using Herschel PACS/SPIRE and JCMT SCUBA-2 observations from 70 to $850\,μ\mathrm{m}$. We model the dust emission using both single-temperature modified blackbody (SMBB) fits and point process mapping (PPMAP), comparing pixel-by-pixel SED-fitting with image cubes of dust surface density as a function of position and temperature. For fixed $β= 1.9$ and a dust opacity of $κ_{350\,μ\mathrm{m}} = 1.92\,\mathrm{cm}^{2}\,\mathrm{g}^{-1}$, SMBB gives an integrated dust mass of $(1.77 \pm 0.09) \times 10^{7}\,M_\odot$, while PPMAP gives $(2.65 \pm 0.13) \times10^{7}\,M_\odot$. The higher PPMAP mass is expected because real lines of sight contain dust over a range of temperatures, whereas SMBB assumes a single effective temperature and can underestimate the dust mass. Both methods show enhanced dust surface densities along the spiral arms and a radially declining dust temperature, with the warmest dust in the central region. Variable-$β$ fits indicate only moderate spatial variation in $β$ for well-constrained pixels, but the strong $T$-$β$ degeneracy motivates a fixed emissivity index for the main analysis. Combining the dust maps with HI data, we find a positive radial gas-to-dust ratio gradient, with $d\log_{10}(\mathrm{GDR})/dR = 0.065\,\mathrm{dex}\,\mathrm{kpc}^{-1}$. Comparison with M81's metallicity gradient implies a declining dust-to-metals ratio, potentially consistent with more efficient grain growth in the inner disc. The star formation rate is modest, $\sim 0.27\,M_\odot\,{\rm yr}^{-1}$, and is strongly concentrated along the spiral arms. These results suggest that the dust, gas, and star-forming structures of M81 are strongly shaped by its spiral arms, while the central region hosts the warmest dust in the disc.

AI.tldr: This paper maps dust in the nearby spiral galaxy M81 from 70 to 850 μm using Herschel and JCMT observations, comparing single-temperature modified blackbody (SMBB) fits with point process mapping (PPMAP), and combines the dust maps with HI data to study dust mass, temperature, gas-to-dust ratio gradients, and star formation.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to characterize the resolved dust properties of M81 and test how SED-fitting methodology (SMBB vs. PPMAP) affects inferred dust mass, given that real lines of sight contain dust over a range of temperatures.
AI.method: They use Herschel PACS/SPIRE and JCMT SCUBA-2 far-infrared/sub-mm imaging (70-850 μm), fitting dust emission with SMBB (fixed β=1.9, κ_350μm=1.92 cm² g⁻¹) and PPMAP, comparing pixel-by-pixel SED fits with dust surface density image cubes. Variable-β fits probe spatial variation in the emissivity index. Dust maps are combined with HI data to derive the gas-to-dust ratio gradient and compared with the metallicity gradient.
AI.result: SMBB yields an integrated dust mass of (1.77 ± 0.09) × 10⁷ M☉, while PPMAP gives (2.65 ± 0.13) × 10⁷ M☉; the higher PPMAP value reflects temperature mixing along the line of sight that SMBB underestimates. Both methods show enhanced dust surface density along spiral arms and a radially declining dust temperature with warmest dust centrally. Variable-β fits show only moderate spatial variation for well-constrained pixels. The gas-to-dust ratio has a positive radial gradient, dlog₁₀(GDR)/dR = 0.065 dex kpc⁻¹, implying a declining dust-to-metals ratio consistent with more efficient grain growth in the inner disc. The SFR is ~0.27 M☉ yr⁻¹, concentrated along the spiral arms.
AI.conclusion: The dust, gas, and star-forming structures of M81 are strongly shaped by its spiral arms, while the central region hosts the warmest dust in the disc. Methodology choice materially affects dust mass estimates, and the inferred dust-to-metals gradient hints at radially varying grain growth efficiency.

title: MP-DualNet: A Dual-Branch Deep Learning Approach for Magnetopause Boundary Detection Using Simulated SXI Images
summary: The Earth's magnetopause is a key boundary governing solar wind-magnetosphere coupling. The Solar wind Magnetosphere Ionosphere Link Explorer (SMILE) mission will provide global soft X-ray imaging of the magnetosphere through solar wind charge exchange (SWCX) emission, offering a new opportunity for remote sensing of magnetopause dynamics. However, the limited field of view (FOV) and variable observation geometry of the Soft X-ray Imager (SXI) pose challenges for reliable magnetopause detection. In this study, we develop MP-DualNet, an end-to-end dual-branch deep learning framework for automated magnetopause detection from simulated SXI observations. The framework jointly performs coarse localization to determine magnetopause visibility and relative position within the FOV, and fine-scale boundary localization through pixel-level segmentation. The model is trained and evaluated using line-of-sight magnetopause envelope maps derived from global hybrid simulations under different solar wind and interplanetary magnetic field conditions. The results demonstrate stable and consistent performance, with a classification accuracy exceeding 0.94 and a segmentation IoU above 0.97. For the test set, the mean absolute angular displacement from the reference boundary was 0.488 degrees. The model maintains robust performance across a wide range of noise levels and generalizes well, as demonstrated by its application to an independent storm event. These results indicate that MP-DualNet provides a reliable and generalizable approach for magnetopause detection in SXI observations, supporting future 3D reconstruction and space weather studies in the context of the SMILE mission.

AI.tldr: MP-DualNet: an end-to-end dual-branch deep learning framework for automated magnetopause detection from simulated SMILE/SXI soft X-ray observations, combining coarse visibility localization and pixel-level boundary segmentation.
AI.motivation: The magnetopause governs solar wind-magnetosphere coupling. SMILE will provide global soft X-ray imaging via solar wind charge exchange (SWCX), enabling remote sensing of magnetopause dynamics, but the SXI's limited field of view and variable observation geometry make reliable automated magnetopause detection challenging.
AI.method: A dual-branch deep learning framework performing (1) coarse localization to determine magnetopause visibility and relative position within the FOV, and (2) fine-scale boundary localization via pixel-level segmentation. Trained and evaluated on line-of-sight magnetopause envelope maps derived from global hybrid simulations under varying solar wind and IMF conditions.
AI.result: Classification accuracy >0.94; segmentation IoU >0.97; mean absolute angular displacement from the reference boundary of 0.488° on the test set. Performance is robust across a wide range of noise levels and generalizes to an independent storm event.
AI.conclusion: MP-DualNet offers a reliable and generalizable approach for magnetopause detection in SXI observations, supporting future 3D reconstruction and space weather studies within the SMILE mission.

title: The HST-Hyperion Survey: X-ray AGN Enhancement in the Hyperion Proto-supercluster
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures. Submitted to ApJL
summary: Dense environments can influence both galaxy evolution and supermassive black hole growth, but whether they enhance or suppress (or both) active galactic nuclei (AGN) activity at high redshift ($z\gtrsim2$) remains uncertain. As one of the most massive structures identified in the early universe, the Hyperion proto-supercluster at $z\approx2.5$ provides a unique opportunity to investigate this connection during an epoch near the peak of both cosmic star formation rate and AGN activity density. To examine the impact of galaxy environment on AGN activity, we measure the fraction of X-ray-selected AGN in Hyperion as a whole, its highly overdense peaks, and its outskirts, comparing these measurements to a coeval field sample. We identify X-ray AGN using the deep Chandra COSMOS-Legacy Survey and combine optical/near-infrared (NIR) photometry and photometric redshift information from COSMOS2020 with extensive ground-based spectroscopy and HST-grism observations. Redshift information is incorporated statistically using a Monte Carlo framework. We find a higher X-ray AGN fraction in Hyperion ($7.4^{+3.2}_{-1.8}\%$) than in the coeval field ($3.2^{+0.6}_{-0.5}\%$), corresponding to a $\sim2.3σ$ difference. Strikingly, this enhancement is concentrated in the overdense peaks, where the X-ray AGN fraction reaches $12.3^{+5.5}_{-3.4}\%$ ($15.0^{+6.9}_{-4.4}\%$ in the most massive peaks versus $6.2^{+11.9}_{-2.1}\%$ in the less massive peaks), while the lower-density Hyperion outskirts ($2.1^{+3.6}_{-1.1}\%$) show no evidence of enhancement relative to the field. These results add to the limited but growing evidence for enhanced AGN activity in high-redshift protostructures, suggesting that the dense environments at these epochs may preferentially trigger AGN during the early stages of cluster assembly.

AI.tldr: Using deep Chandra COSMOS-Legacy X-ray data combined with COSMOS2020 photometry and spectroscopy, the authors measure an elevated X-ray AGN fraction in the z≈2.5 Hyperion proto-supercluster (7.4%) relative to the coeval field (3.2%), with the enhancement concentrated in overdense peaks (12.3–15.0%) and absent in the outskirts.
AI.motivation: Whether dense environments enhance or suppress AGN activity at high redshift (z≳2) is unresolved; Hyperion, a massive proto-supercluster at z≈2.5 near the peak epoch of cosmic star formation and AGN activity density, offers a unique testbed for the environment–AGN connection.
AI.method: X-ray AGN are identified via the deep Chandra COSMOS-Legacy Survey, combined with COSMOS2020 optical/NIR photometry and photometric redshifts, extensive ground-based spectroscopy, and HST-grism observations. Redshift information is incorporated statistically through a Monte Carlo framework. AGN fractions are computed for Hyperion as a whole, its overdense peaks, and its outskirts, and compared to a coeval field sample.
AI.result: The X-ray AGN fraction is higher in Hyperion (7.4^{+3.2}_{-1.8}%) than in the coeval field (3.2^{+0.6}_{-0.5}%), a ~2.3σ difference. The enhancement is concentrated in overdense peaks, reaching 12.3^{+5.5}_{-3.4}% (15.0^{+6.9}_{-4.4}% in the most massive peaks vs. 6.2^{+11.9}_{-2.1}% in less massive peaks), while the low-density outskirts (2.1^{+3.6}_{-1.1}%) show no enhancement relative to the field.
AI.conclusion: The findings add to growing evidence for enhanced AGN activity in high-redshift protostructures, suggesting that dense environments at these epochs may preferentially trigger AGN during the early stages of cluster assembly.

authors: David L. Kaplan Patrick A. Woudt
title: Systematic Search for Cataclysmic Variables in Radio Surveys: First Radio Detection of IX Velorum
comment: 25 pages, 7 figures, 2 MRT tables (Tables 1 & A1), Submitted to ApJ
summary: We present a systematic search for radio emission from cataclysmic variables (CVs) across four wide-field radio surveys in the 0.7-4 GHz frequency range: VLASS; RACS; VAST; and EMU. We generated a reliable catalog of 2225 optically-identified CV candidates using a multi-stage cross-match, combined with systematic and manual verification; 1374 are matched to Gaia sources within the radio surveys' footprints. Among these, we detected six CVs in at least one epoch (at 1e16.5-1e17.5 erg/s/Hz, consistent with the typical population of radio-detected CVs); five had been detected in radio before. IX Vel, the closest nova-like CV, is detected in radio for the first time and shows quasi-persistent low-level emission across a 10 hr EMU (943.5 MHz) observation. Given most epochs detected no CV, we stacked images without radio detections to better constrain time-averaged brightnesses. We created co-added images and placed upper limits on low-level radio emission from each of the 423 individual CVs within the VAST footprint. To constrain the median brightness for the entire CV population, we combined all Gaia-matched CVs in each survey into single population-wide stacked images, detecting no statistically significant emission. Finally, we created population-wide image stacks of the CVs within 100 pc, using 14 epochs from 5 CVs in EMU to constrain their median persistent specific luminosity to <3e14 erg/s/Hz.

AI.tldr: A systematic search across four wide-field radio surveys yields a 2225-source optically-identified CV catalog; six CVs are detected, IX Vel is newly detected, and population stacking constrains median persistent luminosity to <3e14 erg/s/Hz.
AI.motivation: Radio emission from cataclysmic variables (CVs) remains poorly characterized at population level; a systematic, wide-field census is needed to establish detection rates and median brightnesses.
AI.method: Cross-matched 2225 optically-identified CV candidates (1374 Gaia-matched) against VLASS, RACS, VAST, and EMU (0.7-4 GHz) via multi-stage matching with systematic and manual verification; stacked non-detections into co-added images, including per-source stacks for 423 CVs in VAST and population-wide stacks per survey, plus a 100 pc sample (14 epochs, 5 CVs in EMU).
AI.result: Six CVs detected in at least one epoch at 1e16.5-1e17.5 erg/s/Hz (five previously known); IX Vel newly detected with quasi-persistent low-level emission over a 10 hr EMU observation at 943.5 MHz; population-wide stacks show no significant emission; median persistent specific luminosity of nearby CVs constrained to <3e14 erg/s/Hz.
AI.conclusion: Radio-detected CVs are rare and consistent with an established brightness range; stacking places stringent upper limits on time-averaged and median persistent radio emission, indicating most CVs are faint radio sources below current survey sensitivity.

title: The ALPINE-CRISTAL-JWST Survey: The Tully-Fisher Relation at $z = 4-6$
comment: 13 pages, 6 Figures, 2 Tables, Accepted for Publication in A&A
summary: The Tully-Fisher relation provides a fundamental link between galaxy mass and their kinematics. Although its evolution is relatively well constrained up to cosmic noon, observational probes at higher redshifts remain scarce. In this work, we investigate the stellar and baryonic Tully-Fisher relations (TFRs) at $z=4-6$ by analyzing JWST/NIRSpec IFU observations of 18 main-sequence star-forming galaxies belonging to the ALPINE-CRISTAL-JWST survey. We apply a morpho-kinematic disk classification scheme, finding five disk-like galaxies and a survey disk fraction of $0.28\pm0.11$. These disk galaxies span stellar masses of $10^{9.5-10.5}\,M_\odot$, intrinsic rotational velocities of $91-127\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}}$, and intrinsic velocity dispersions of $66-129\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}}$. For both versions of the TFR, we find that the ALPINE-CRISTAL-JWST disks lie below the local relations and are likely offset from those reported at cosmic noon ($z\approx2.3$). By fixing the TFR slope to the $z=0$ value, we measure zero-point offsets for the stellar-mass TFR of $-0.96\pm0.18$ dex and $-0.50\pm0.18$ dex relative to the local Universe and cosmic noon, respectively. For the baryonic TFR, we find zero-point offsets of $-0.57\pm0.20$ dex and $-0.30\pm0.20$ dex with respect to the local Universe and cosmic noon relations. Our measurements are consistent with the redshift evolution of the zero-points of both TFRs being driven by the evolution of dark matter halo properties with cosmic time, modulated by a reduced contribution of dark matter to the dynamical mass on the galaxy scale.

AI.tldr: JWST/NIRSpec IFU observations of 18 ALPINE-CRISTAL-JWST galaxies at z=4-6 yield five disk-like galaxies (disk fraction 0.28±0.11); their stellar and baryonic TFRs lie below local and cosmic-noon relations, with zero-point offsets consistent with dark-matter halo evolution plus reduced inner dark-matter fraction.
AI.motivation: The Tully-Fisher relation links galaxy mass to kinematics and is well constrained up to cosmic noon, but observational probes at higher redshift (z>3) remain scarce, leaving the high-redshift evolution of the stellar and baryonic TFRs poorly tested.
AI.method: Analysis of JWST/NIRSpec IFU spectroscopy for 18 main-sequence star-forming galaxies from the ALPINE-CRISTAL-JWST survey at z=4-6. A morpho-kinematic disk classification scheme is applied to identify rotating disks and derive intrinsic rotational velocities and velocity dispersions. Stellar and baryonic TFR zero-points are measured with the slope fixed to the z=0 value and compared with local and z≈2.3 relations.
AI.result: Five disk-like galaxies are identified, giving a disk fraction of 0.28±0.11, with stellar masses 10^9.5-10.5 M_sun, intrinsic rotational velocities 91-127 km/s, and intrinsic velocity dispersions 66-129 km/s. Both TFRs lie below the local relations and are likely offset from cosmic noon. Zero-point offsets: stellar TFR -0.96±0.18 dex (vs z=0) and -0.50±0.18 dex (vs z≈2.3); baryonic TFR -0.57±0.20 dex and -0.30±0.20 dex, respectively.
AI.conclusion: The measured offsets are consistent with the redshift evolution of both TFR zero-points being driven by the evolution of dark matter halo properties with cosmic time, modulated by a reduced contribution of dark matter to the dynamical mass on galaxy scales.

title: Thorium and Europium production in the early Galaxy: Implications for nucleocosmochronology
comment: 15 pages, accepted for publication in A&A
summary:
The ages of the oldest stellar populations can be investigated through nucleocosmochronology, with the thorium-to-europium abundance ratio providing a promising chronometer. We assess the reliability of log(Th/Eu) as an age indicator by testing whether thorium and europium were co-produced in a constant ratio in metal-poor stars, and evaluate the uncertainties affecting stellar ages.
  We present new Th and Eu abundance measurements for eight TITANS reference stars observed with UVES at the VLT. Combining these measurements with homogeneous literature samples, we investigate the behaviour of log(Th/Eu) as a function of metallicity. We derive ages adopting a theoretical initial r-process production ratio and assess the effects of observational uncertainties and sample statistics.
  At low metallicity, the observed Th/Eu ratios show no significant dependence on metallicity after excluding stars with anomalous actinide abundances, supporting broadly uniform Th and Eu co-production in the early Galaxy. The derived ages are consistent with expectations for an old, metal-poor halo population, although individual uncertainties remain substantial. Higher spectral resolution is needed to improve Th measurements, while combining stars in coeval populations can provide additional statistical gains.
  Nucleocosmochronology offers an independent approach to dating the oldest stellar populations. Homogeneous samples of coeval stars, particularly in globular clusters, observed with future high-resolution multi-object spectrographs could provide stronger constraints on the early formation history of the Milky Way and the age of the Universe.

AI.tldr: This study tests the thorium-to-europium abundance ratio log(Th/Eu) as a nucleocosmochronological age indicator using new UVES/VLT measurements of eight TITANS reference stars, finding consistent co-production at low metallicity and plausible old-halo ages despite substantial individual uncertainties.
AI.motivation: The ages of the oldest stellar populations require independent dating methods; nucleocosmochronology via the Th/Eu ratio is promising but its reliability depends on whether Th and Eu were co-produced in a constant ratio in metal-poor stars and on the magnitude of the uncertainties involved.
AI.method: New Th and Eu abundance measurements for eight TITANS reference stars observed with UVES at the VLT are presented and combined with homogeneous literature samples. The behavior of log(Th/Eu) as a function of metallicity is examined, ages are derived assuming a theoretical initial r-process production ratio, and the impact of observational errors and sample statistics is assessed.
AI.result: At low metallicity, observed Th/Eu ratios show no significant metallicity dependence once stars with anomalous actinide abundances are excluded, supporting broadly uniform early-Galaxy Th and Eu co-production. Derived ages match expectations for an old metal-poor halo population, but individual uncertainties remain large; higher spectral resolution and statistical averaging over coeval stars are needed for improvement.
AI.conclusion: Nucleocosmochronology provides an independent route to dating the oldest stellar populations. Homogeneous samples of coeval stars—especially in globular clusters—observed with future high-resolution multi-object spectrographs could yield stronger constraints on the early formation history of the Milky Way and on the age of the Universe.

Using the infrared data from the Spitzer Space Telescope and the Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer, we find a spatial correlation between the locations of massive stars and the distribution of young stellar objects, indicating a possible sequential pattern of star formation across the region. These results indicate the role of massive-star feedback in shaping the star-formation history of the complex

AI.tldr: Using Spitzer and WISE infrared data, the study finds a spatial correlation between massive stars and young stellar objects in the BRC 44 / LDN 1204 region of Cepheus OB2, suggesting sequential star formation driven by massive-star feedback.
AI.motivation: OB2 associations are ideal laboratories for studying star-formation processes; prior work on BRC 44 hinted at triggered star formation via radiative feedback, motivating a broader investigation of the region between the H II regions Sh2-140 and Sh2-145.
AI.method: Analysis of infrared data from the Spitzer Space Telescope and the Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE), examining the spatial distribution of young stellar objects relative to massive stars in the bright-rimmed cloud BRC 44 and the dark cloud LDN 1204.
AI.result: A spatial correlation is found between the locations of massive stars and the distribution of young stellar objects across the region, indicating a possible sequential pattern of star formation.

title: Cepheid Metallicity in the Leavitt Law (C-MetaLL) survey: X First spectroscopic characterization of Galactic Type II Cepheids and calibration of the Period-Wesenheit-Metallicity relations
comment: Article proposed for acceptance in Astronomy & Astrophysics. 12 pages, 8 figures, 8 tables
summary:
Type II Cepheids (T2Cs) are Population II pulsating stars that serve as distance indicators through their period--luminosity relation. Along with RR Lyrae stars and the tip of the red giant branch, they offer an independent route to the Hubble constant, helping assess systematic uncertainties in its determination.
  We aim to investigate the impact of chemical composition on T2Cs' period--luminosity relations by building a homogeneous spectroscopic sample of Galactic T2Cs with iron and oxygen abundances.
  We observed 80 Galactic T2Cs with UVES at the ESO Very Large Telescope. For 74 stars, we derived stellar parameters and iron and oxygen abundances through a self-consistent spectroscopic analysis based on equivalent widths of absorption lines. This sample nearly doubles the number of T2Cs with spectroscopic metallicity measurements available in the literature.
  We used these abundances to test theoretical predictions for the instability strip and, together with $Gaia$ parallaxes, to derive Period--Wesenheit--metallicity (PWZ) relations. In agreement with theoretical predictions, the metallicity coefficient ($γ$) is small and statistically consistent with zero in all relations, ranging from approximately $-0.02$ to $+0.17$ mag dex$^{-1}$. We also estimated distances to 22 Galactic Globular Clusters hosting T2Cs, finding agreement within uncertainties with independent literature estimates.
  Our results show that metallicity has, at most, a minor impact on T2Cs' pulsation properties and distance scale, supporting their reliability as Population II distance indicators.

AI.tldr: A homogeneous spectroscopic sample of 80 Galactic Type II Cepheids (74 with derived parameters and Fe/O abundances) nearly doubles literature data and shows that metallicity has at most a minor effect on their period–luminosity (Wesenheit) relations, supporting their use as Population II distance indicators.
AI.motivation: Type II Cepheids are Population II distance indicators that, together with RR Lyrae stars and the red giant branch tip, provide an independent route to the Hubble constant and help quantify its systematic uncertainties. The influence of chemical composition on their period–luminosity relations needs clarification.
AI.method: Observed 80 Galactic T2Cs with UVES at the ESO VLT. For 74 stars, derived stellar parameters and iron and oxygen abundances via self-consistent spectroscopic analysis using equivalent widths of absorption lines. Abundances were used to test instability-strip predictions and, combined with Gaia parallaxes, to derive Period–Wesenheit–metallicity (PWZ) relations. Distances to 22 Galactic globular clusters hosting T2Cs were also estimated.
AI.result: The metallicity coefficient γ is small and statistically consistent with zero across all relations (roughly −0.02 to +0.17 mag dex⁻¹), in agreement with theoretical predictions. Cluster distances agree within uncertainties with independent literature estimates.
AI.conclusion: Metallicity has at most a minor impact on T2C pulsation properties and the distance scale, supporting their reliability as Population II distance indicators and their role in testing the Hubble constant.

title: Formamide formation on forsterite and Mg(OH)$_2\cdot$H$_2$O
comment: 18 pages, 10 figures. Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: Context. Formamide formation in the Universe has been the subject of debate due to its importance as a precursor to amino acids and RNA. Current studies focus on the gas-phase and icy grain formation routes. However, formamide formation on bare silicate surfaces or hydrated Mg-bearing molecular models remains largely unexplored in environments relevant to protoplanetary disks. Aims. This study presents a quantum-chemical investigation of formamide formation on an Mg center and a silicate surface. $Mg(OH)_2\cdot H_2O$ and the bare (010) forsterite ($Mg_2SiO_4$) surface, used as an analog of a bare dust-grain surface, may promote formamide formation via $NH_2$ addition to $H_2CO$. Methods. I employed density functional theory (DFT) to study the addition of $NH_2$ to $H_2CO$ with an isolated $Mg(OH)_2\cdot H_2O$ molecular model and on the forsterite (010) surface. First, I benchmarked various theoretical methodologies. I then examined the ability of $Mg(OH)_2\cdot H_2O$ and the forsterite (010) surface to promote formamide formation. Finally, for the case with an entrance barrier, I computed unimolecular rate constants and half-lives to assess its kinetic behavior. Results. $Mg(OH)_2\cdot H_2O$ promotes proton transfer within the $NH_2$-$CH_2O$ intermediate via the O-H group coordinated with Mg following $NH_2$ addition to $H_2CO$, whereas on the forsterite, a barrier-less addition pathway is found when $NH_2$ is initially physisorbed close to the formaldehyde center, followed by proton transfer leading to formamide formation. Conclusions. The Mg-bearing model systems considered here can promote rapid proton transfer following $NH_2$ addition to $H_2CO$. For the $Mg(OH)_2\cdot H_2O$ model, the reaction step from the pre-reactive complex is predicted to occur on nanosecond timescales at temperatures approaching 300 K. The present work provides kinetic data for astrochemical models.

AI.tldr: DFT study shows that Mg-bearing models ($Mg(OH)_2\cdot H_2O$ and bare forsterite (010) surface) promote formamide formation via $NH_2$ addition to $H_2CO$ followed by rapid proton transfer, with nanosecond-timescale kinetics near 300 K, providing data for astrochemical models.
AI.motivation: Formamide is a key precursor to amino acids and RNA, but its formation routes have mainly been studied in the gas phase and on icy grains; formation on bare silicate surfaces or hydrated Mg-bearing molecular models relevant to protoplanetary disks remains largely unexplored.
AI.method: Density functional theory (DFT) benchmarked across several methodologies was used to study $NH_2$ addition to $H_2CO$ on an isolated $Mg(OH)_2\cdot H_2O$ molecular model and on the bare (010) forsterite ($Mg_2SiO_4$) surface (dust-grain analog). For pathways with an entrance barrier, unimolecular rate constants and half-lives were computed.
AI.result: On $Mg(OH)_2\cdot H_2O$, proton transfer within the $NH_2$-$CH_2O$ intermediate proceeds via the Mg-coordinated O-H group after $NH_2$ addition. On forsterite, a barrier-less addition pathway occurs when $NH_2$ is physisorbed near the formaldehyde center, followed by proton transfer yielding formamide. For the $Mg(OH)_2\cdot H_2O$ model, the reaction step from the pre-reactive complex is predicted on nanosecond timescales near 300 K.
AI.conclusion: Mg-bearing model systems can promote rapid proton transfer following $NH_2$ addition to $H_2CO$, supporting formamide synthesis on silicate/Mg-containing dust surfaces; the computed kinetic data are intended for astrochemical models.

title: Survey of Surveys Data Release 3. Homogenised stellar parameters across nine spectroscopic surveys
comment: Submitted to A&A. 20 pages, 17 figures, 5 tables
summary: Large spectroscopic surveys have measured atmospheric parameters for millions of Milky Way stars, but differences in instruments, wavelength ranges, analysis methods, and assumptions introduce survey-dependent systematics that complicate their joint use. We aim to place effective temperature, surface gravity, and metallicity estimates from major spectroscopic surveys onto a common, externally validated scale, and to provide a homogenised catalogue for large-scale Galactic studies. We construct the calibration hierarchically. We first define an internal reference scale from the best-populated and best-overlapped surveys (APOGEE, GALAH, and LAMOST LRS), and model survey-to-reference corrections and their uncertainties with machine-learning regression. The scale is then extended to LAMOST MRS, Gaia RVS, RAVE, DESI, Gaia-ESO, and SEGUE, and anchored to high-quality measurements from the PASTEL database. The calibration reduces survey-to-survey offsets and improves consistency in independent overlap samples: independent calibration of GALAH and LAMOST LRS temperatures onto the APOGEE scale reduces their median offset from 44.5 K to 6.2 K. The final catalogue contains about 10.13 million stars, including 6.10 million in the recommended high-quality subset and 3.69 million in the metallicity-optimised subset. For the high-quality subset, Gaia benchmark stars give median residuals of 30 K in $T_{\rm eff}$, 0.03 dex in $\log g$, and $-0.02$ dex in [Fe/H]. The [Fe/H]-optimised subset gives median residuals of 0.003 dex against Gaia benchmark stars, 0.05 dex for globular clusters, and $-0.02$ dex for open clusters. As an example application, we confirm the presence of metal-poor stars on thin-disc-like orbits, including stars with [Fe/H] $< -2$, showing that the catalogue can be used to study rare Galactic populations on a consistent multi-survey scale.

AI.tldr: A hierarchical machine-learning calibration places atmospheric parameters from major spectroscopic surveys onto a common, externally validated scale, producing a homogenised catalogue of ~10.13 million stars for large-scale Galactic studies.
AI.motivation: Millions of stellar atmospheric parameters exist from large spectroscopic surveys, but differences in instruments, wavelength ranges, analysis methods and assumptions create survey-dependent systematics that hamper their joint use. A common, externally validated scale is needed.
AI.method: Hierarchical calibration: (1) define an internal reference scale from the best-populated, best-overlapped surveys (APOGEE, GALAH, LAMOST LRS); (2) model survey-to-reference corrections and their uncertainties with machine-learning regression; (3) extend the scale to LAMOST MRS, Gaia RVS, RAVE, DESI, Gaia-ESO and SEGUE; (4) anchor to high-quality PASTEL measurements.
AI.result: Offsets are reduced and consistency improved in independent overlap samples: independently calibrating GALAH and LAMOST LRS temperatures onto the APOGEE scale cuts their median offset from 44.5 K to 6.2 K. The catalogue holds ~10.13 million stars (6.10 million high-quality subset; 3.69 million metallicity-optimised subset). High-quality subset vs Gaia benchmark stars: median residuals 30 K in Teff, 0.03 dex in log g, -0.02 dex in [Fe/H]. [Fe/H]-optimised subset: 0.003 dex vs Gaia benchmarks, 0.05 dex for globular clusters, -0.02 dex for open clusters.
AI.conclusion: The homogenised multi-survey catalogue is externally validated and applicable to rare Galactic populations; as a demonstration, metal-poor stars ([Fe/H] < -2) on thin-disc-like orbits are confirmed.

title: CosmicGrain: An On-the-fly Dust Physics Module
summary: We present CosmicGrain, a dust physics module built on Gadget-4 that models explicit dust superparticles that experience resolved gas-dust drag and radiation pressure, undergo collisional heating and cooling with gas, and are further shaped by subgrid treatments for grain growth, thermal sputtering, coagulation, shattering, supernova shock destruction, and astration. We run an eleven-rung physics ladder (S0-S10) at 1024^3 resolution to isolate the contribution of individual processes to a Milky Way-mass halo's dust population. Because dust is evolved as active on-the-fly particles, individual grains retain distinct histories producing results inaccessible to passive dust models such as the strongly asymmetric silicate-to-carbon shattering destruction ratio driven by silicate grains' smaller birth size. Gas-dust drag is the dominant driver of ISM dust enrichment, increasing dust levels by ~100 times while every other process changes the R200 dust abundance by only 10-30%. We find reasonable agreement with the Milky Way's radial dust-to-gas and dust-to-metal ratios, with carbon dust preferentially enriching the CGM relative to silicates. The code is freely available at https://cosmicgrain.space.

AI.tldr: CosmicGrain is a Gadget-4-based dust physics module using explicit dust superparticles with resolved drag, radiation pressure, and subgrid grain processing; an 11-stage physics ladder shows gas-dust drag dominates ISM dust enrichment (~100x), while on-the-fly grain evolution reveals asymmetric silicate/carbon shattering behavior and preferential carbon enrichment of the CGM.
AI.motivation: Passive dust models cannot track individual grain histories, so the relative importance of individual dust processes and grain-species-dependent effects in a Milky Way-mass halo remains unclear. The authors seek to isolate each physical process's contribution to the dust population.
AI.method: Built CosmicGrain on Gadget-4 with explicit dust superparticles experiencing resolved gas-dust drag and radiation pressure, collisional heating/cooling with gas, plus subgrid grain growth, thermal sputtering, coagulation, shattering, supernova shock destruction, and astration. Ran an eleven-rung physics ladder (S0-S10) at 1024^3 resolution on a Milky Way-mass halo.
AI.result: Gas-dust drag dominates ISM dust enrichment, raising dust levels ~100x, while all other processes change R200 dust abundance by only 10-30%. On-the-fly particle evolution yields a strongly asymmetric silicate-to-carbon shattering destruction ratio (due to silicates' smaller birth size). Results agree reasonably with the Milky Way's radial dust-to-gas and dust-to-metal ratios, with carbon dust preferentially enriching the CGM relative to silicates.
AI.conclusion: Explicit active dust particles capture grain-history-dependent physics inaccessible to passive models. Gas-dust drag is the key driver of ISM dust enrichment in a Milky Way-mass halo, and grain species differentially enrich the CGM, with carbon favored over silicates. The code is publicly available.

title: Mass loss in AF supergiants: At the verge of the Eddington limit and still with weak line-driven winds
comment: 13 pages, accepted for publication in A&A
summary: We study global atmosphere models of AF supergiants. In agreement with previous studies, we found super-Eddington layers in the photospheres of these stars, which lead to density inversions. Our tests showed that the super-Eddington layers are caused by hydrogen ionization. The analysis of radial perturbations has not revealed any instability of such layers, but we show that super-Eddington layers in an optically thick environment are prone to instabilities due to nonradial perturbations. We predict the wind parameters of AF supergiants from our global wind code with a comoving-frame radiative force. Despite the existence of density inversions, the predicted mass-loss rates are significantly lower than those estimated from observations. Theoretical values approach the observational estimates only for the most luminous supergiants, which are close to the Eddington limit due to light scattering on free electrons. Part of the discrepancy between the mass-loss rates could be attributed to the influence of the clumping on the observational properties. Low mass-loss rates imply that the winds of AF supergiants may be strongly influenced by the magnetic fields, suggesting an explanation for the observed spectral variability of these stars.

AI.tldr: Global atmosphere models of AF supergiants reveal super-Eddington layers (driven by hydrogen ionization) that cause density inversions. These layers are stable to radial but unstable to nonradial perturbations. Predicted mass-loss rates are significantly below observational estimates except for the most luminous, Eddington-approaching stars; clumping and magnetic fields may reconcile the discrepancy and explain spectral variability.
AI.motivation: To understand the atmospheric structure and wind properties of AF supergiants, particularly the origin and stability of super-Eddington layers and the persistent mismatch between theoretical and observed mass-loss rates.
AI.method: Global atmosphere modeling of AF supergiants; stability analysis of super-Eddington layers under radial and nonradial perturbations; global wind modeling with a comoving-frame radiative force to predict wind parameters.
AI.result: Super-Eddington layers in the photospheres are confirmed and attributed to hydrogen ionization, producing density inversions. Radial perturbation analysis shows no instability, whereas nonradial perturbations destabilize super-Eddington layers in optically thick environments. Predicted mass-loss rates are significantly lower than observed values, approaching observations only for the most luminous supergiants near the Eddington limit via electron scattering.
AI.conclusion: The mass-loss discrepancy may partly stem from clumping effects on observational diagnostics. The low theoretical mass-loss rates imply that magnetic fields could strongly influence AF supergiant winds, offering a possible explanation for their observed spectral variability.

title: GetGaia 2.0: automatic membership and systemic motions of stellar systems with Gaia
comment: 22 pages, 17 figures, 8 tables. Submitted to A&A. The code will be available at https://github.com/AndresdPM/GetGaia2
summary: We present GetGaia 2.0, a public Python package that retrieves the Gaia data around a stellar system and selects its member stars automatically. The membership is a probabilistic model fitted by expectation maximization that combines the astrometry of every source, with its full covariance, the color-magnitude diagram, the sky distribution and, when available, the line-of-sight velocities, from Gaia or from an external catalog. The local systematic errors of the Gaia reference frame are measured on the quasars of each field. The code returns the systemic proper motion (PM) and parallax with their full covariance, a detection significance, a contamination estimate and the structural parameters of the system. We validate it on synthetic catalogs, where it recovers the members with 90-100 percent purity, and run it on Gaia DR3 for the known dwarf galaxies of the Local Group within 850 kpc and for 95 Galactic globular clusters, in tiers that add one piece of literature information at a time. It measures the systemic PMs of 55 dwarf galaxies and 93 globular clusters at a significance of at least $3σ$; 29 of the dwarfs and 86 of the clusters are recovered from their position alone. The dwarfs include every Milky Way satellite within 300 kpc brighter than $M_V=-5.4$, ultra-faint systems down to $M_V=-0.8$, and nine galaxies at 370-820 kpc. The PMs agree with the published values within 0.1 mas/yr for 47 of the dwarfs and for all the clusters (median differences of 0.032 and 0.009 mas/yr), with uncertainties equal to those of dedicated studies, and none deviates by more than $3σ$. The Gaia line-of-sight velocities alone give the systemic velocity of 71 clusters, within 1 km/s of spectroscopy. GetGaia 2.0 delivers, without manual intervention, the systemic motions and the members of the stellar systems within the reach of Gaia, and is ready for the forthcoming Gaia data releases.

AI.tldr: GetGaia 2.0 is a public Python package that automatically retrieves Gaia data around stellar systems and selects member stars via an expectation-maximization probabilistic model, returning systemic proper motion, parallax, detection significance, contamination and structural parameters without manual intervention.
AI.motivation: Selecting member stars and measuring systemic motion of stellar systems (dwarf galaxies, globular clusters) from Gaia data typically requires manual, per-object effort. The authors seek an automated, reproducible pipeline that combines all available observables to deliver systemic astrometry for any system within Gaia's reach, including faint and distant ones.
AI.method: A probabilistic membership model fitted by expectation maximization combining per-source astrometry with full covariance, the color-magnitude diagram, sky distribution, and line-of-sight velocities from Gaia or external catalogs. Local systematic errors of the Gaia reference frame are measured on quasars in each field. The code returns systemic proper motion and parallax with full covariance, detection significance, contamination estimate, and structural parameters. Validated on synthetic catalogs and applied to Gaia DR3 for Local Group dwarfs within 850 kpc and 95 Galactic globular clusters, in tiers adding literature information incrementally.
AI.result: On synthetic catalogs, members are recovered with 90-100 percent purity. It measures systemic PMs for 55 dwarf galaxies and 93 globular clusters at >=3σ; 29 dwarfs and 86 clusters are recovered from position alone. The dwarfs include every Milky Way satellite within 300 kpc brighter than M_V=-5.4, ultra-faint systems down to M_V=-0.8, and nine galaxies at 370-820 kpc. PMs agree with published values within 0.1 mas/yr for 47 dwarfs and all clusters (median differences 0.032 and 0.009 mas/yr), with uncertainties comparable to dedicated studies and none deviating by more than 3σ. Gaia line-of-sight velocities alone yield systemic velocities for 71 clusters within 1 km/s of spectroscopy.
AI.conclusion: GetGaia 2.0 delivers systemic motions and member catalogs for stellar systems within Gaia's reach fully automatically, matches dedicated studies in accuracy and precision, and is ready for forthcoming Gaia data releases.

title: Photometric eclipse-center variations over the long cycles of Magellanic double-periodic variables
comment: Accepted for publication in Astronomy and Astrophysics
summary: Double-periodic variables (DPVs) are interacting binaries with an orbital modulation and a longer cycle of uncertain origin. I searched for long-cycle-dependent eclipse-center variations in Magellanic DPVs and tested whether changing disk brightness can produce analogous shifts with fixed conjunctions. I analyzed Optical Gravitational Lensing Experiment (OGLE) photometry for 109 eclipsing-DPV candidates. In separate long-phase intervals, I measured centers of eclipses by profile fitting to local flux minima ($Q$) and by shifting a fixed eclipse template ($T$). A single synthetic semidetached DPV provided a separate numerical experiment. Of 49 curated systems with sufficient timing data, 27 show at least one $Q$ or $T$ modulation under the adopted procedure. Some selections depend on the fitting choice, but ten systems retain a selected $Q$ curve with all tested local functions and windows. Three have both estimators selected in both eclipses, without establishing whether conjunction times change. Using local color interpolation, 14 of 16 systems measured in both eclipses are redder at the deeper, phase-0 eclipse. In the artificial system, fixed conjunctions coexist with large photometric shifts and quadrature-brightness changes, although the large tilted-disk cases do not reproduce the selected observed crossing phases. Long-cycle-dependent photometric eclipse-center variations occur in a substantial fraction of the evaluable, curated sample, not necessarily of all DPVs. Circumstellar brightness changes can produce such shifts, but the single artificial system neither fits an observed DPV nor establishes disk tilt as the cause. Genuine conjunction-time changes remain possible in individual objects.

AI.tldr: Long-cycle-dependent eclipse-center shifts are common among evaluable Magellanic double-periodic variables, and circumstellar brightness changes can mimic them even with fixed conjunction times.
AI.motivation: Double-periodic variables are interacting binaries with an orbital modulation plus a longer, unexplained cycle; it was unclear whether eclipse centers (conjunction times) vary across the long cycle, or whether apparent shifts are photometric artifacts.
AI.method: OGLE photometry of 109 eclipsing-DPV candidates was analyzed in separate long-phase intervals, measuring eclipse centers by profile fitting to local flux minima (Q) and by shifting a fixed template (T); one synthetic semidetached DPV served as a numerical experiment, with local color interpolation to test eclipse color behavior.
AI.result: Of 49 curated systems with adequate timing data, 27 show at least one Q or T modulation; ten retain a Q curve across all tested local functions and windows, and three have both estimators selected in both eclipses. 14 of 16 systems measured in both eclipses are redder at the deeper phase-0 eclipse. In the artificial system, fixed conjunctions coexist with large photometric shifts and quadrature-brightness changes, though large tilted-disk cases fail to reproduce observed crossing phases.
AI.conclusion: Long-cycle-dependent eclipse-center variations occur in a substantial fraction of the evaluable curated sample (not necessarily all DPVs); circumstellar brightness changes can produce such shifts, but the single artificial model neither matches an observed DPV nor establishes disk tilt as the cause, and genuine conjunction-time changes remain possible in individual objects.

title: Dust Survival in Lensed Quiescent Galaxies at $z>1$ Depends on How They Quench
comment: Submitted to ApJ. 20 pages, 11 figures
summary: The interstellar medium of massive quiescent galaxies holds key clues to how they quench, yet remain poorly understood. Although dust is expected to be depleted rapidly ($\lesssim$100 Myr) after quenching, some quiescent galaxies host substantial dust reservoirs, raising the question of whether dust survives quenching or is replenished afterward. We present ALMA Band 6 continuum observations ($λ_{\mathrm{rest}}$$>$250$μ$m) of eight strongly-lensed, spectroscopically-selected quiescent galaxies at z$\sim$1-2.5 from the COOL-LAMPS and REQUIEM surveys, plus five archival REQUIEM systems. The sample spans more than two orders of magnitude in dust-to-stellar-mass ratio ($f_{\mathrm{dust}}<10^{-5}$ to $>10^{-3}$), and two galaxies host extended, resolved dust. Comparing $f_{\mathrm{dust}}$ with time since quenching, roughly half the sample, preferentially at higher redshift, is consistent with rapid quenching and harsh dust destruction, while lower-redshift, more slowly quenched systems are consistent with milder destruction, possibly reflecting an evolving dominant quenching mode. The two most dust-rich galaxies exceed even the mildest model destruction tracks, with J1201-3952 retaining the highest $f_{\mathrm{dust}}$ $\sim$1.8 Gyr after quenching. If these systems are truly quiescent, their dust masses approach maximum stellar yields, pointing to ISM grain regrowth and/or TP-AGB dust production. However due to our single-band continuum data, $f_{\mathrm{dust}}$ is uncertain ($\pm$0.3 dex systematic uncertainty from the unknown dust temperature) and we cannot rule out obscured star formation in these two galaxies. Our results suggest that dust survival depends on how galaxies quench: rapid, harsh quenching efficiently destroys dust, while slower, milder quenching can leave dust reservoirs that persist or are replenished long after star formation ceases.

AI.tldr: ALMA Band 6 continuum observations of strongly-lensed quiescent galaxies at z~1-2.5 show that dust survival depends on quenching mode: rapid, harsh quenching destroys dust efficiently, while slower quenching leaves long-lived or replenished dust reservoirs.
AI.motivation: The interstellar medium of massive quiescent galaxies remains poorly understood despite being key to how galaxies quench. Dust should be depleted within ~100 Myr after quenching, yet some quiescent galaxies harbor substantial dust reservoirs, raising the question of whether dust survives quenching or is replenished afterward.
AI.method: ALMA Band 6 continuum observations (rest-frame >250 micron) of eight strongly-lensed, spectroscopically-selected quiescent galaxies at z~1-2.5 from COOL-LAMPS and REQUIEM, plus five archival REQUIEM systems. Dust-to-stellar-mass ratios compared with time since quenching and against dust destruction models.
AI.result: The sample spans >2 orders of magnitude in dust-to-stellar-mass ratio (f_dust < 1e-5 to >1e-3); two galaxies show extended, resolved dust. Roughly half the sample, preferentially at higher redshift, is consistent with rapid quenching and harsh dust destruction, while lower-redshift, more slowly quenched systems fit milder destruction. The two most dust-rich galaxies exceed even the mildest destruction tracks, with J1201-3952 retaining f_dust ~1.8 Gyr after quenching, approaching maximum stellar yields.
AI.conclusion: Dust survival depends on how galaxies quench: rapid, harsh quenching efficiently destroys dust, whereas slower, milder quenching can leave dust reservoirs that persist or are replenished long after star formation ceases. If truly quiescent, the dust-rich systems point to ISM grain regrowth and/or TP-AGB dust production. Caveats: single-band data yield ±0.3 dex systematic uncertainty from unknown dust temperature, and obscured star formation cannot be ruled out in the two dust-rich galaxies.

title: Source Imaging of the Multiple Type-II Solar Radio Bursts and their Multiple CME-Shock Signatures in the Corona
comment: Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal
summary: This study reports the meter-wavelength radio imaging of multiple type-II bursts occurred on 01 October 2011 observed by LEARMONTH radio spectrograph in the frequency range of 180 - 25 MHz, with two coronal shocks from two coronal mass ejections (CMEs) from the nearby active regions lying adjacent to each other. The two CMEs are well observed by STEREO and LASCO FOV. The eruption is associated with the multi-peaked soft X-ray flare erupted from N16W45 (first and second C3 and C6 class flares) and from N09W04 (third one an M Class flare). The first type-II burst starts during the impulsive phase of the first flare and the second type-II burst starts during the peak time of the third flare. The drift rate of the second type-II burst is larger than that of the first type-II burst. The EUV images at AIA 211 reveal the shock-like EUV wave structure along the north-western limb around 09:06 UT, the first type-II appearing around the same time (09:06 UT) confirms the existence of the shock wave and as an outward propagating wave along the disk around 09:55 UT, the second type-II appearing around the same time (09:55 UT) confirms the existence of the shock wave. According to the simultaneous EUV and radio imaging data the radio sources appears along the nose-front of the shock like EUV wave structure for the first type-II burst and for the second type-II burst they are located along the shock flank. The study shows the possibility of two coronal shocks from two CMEs generating the multiple type-II radio bursts. The second event is strongly affected by the projection and scattering effects, the corrections are achieved by applying spherical cone model and 3D Monte Carlo ray-tracing code for turbulent solar environment at fundamental frequency.

AI.tldr: Meter-wavelength radio imaging of two type-II bursts on 01 October 2011 reveals two coronal shocks driven by two CMEs from adjacent active regions, with radio sources located along the shock nose and flank as confirmed by concurrent EUV wave observations.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether multiple type-II radio bursts observed during a single eruptive event can be produced by two distinct coronal shocks driven by two separate CMEs originating from nearby active regions, and to relate the radio emission to the shock geometry and EUV wave structure.
AI.method: LEARMONTH radio spectrograph imaging in the 180–25 MHz range, combined with STEREO and LASCO white-light observations of the two CMEs, SXR flare timing, and AIA 211 Å EUV images. For the second burst, projection and scattering effects were corrected using a spherical cone model and a 3D Monte Carlo ray-tracing code for the turbulent solar environment at the fundamental frequency.
AI.result: The first type-II burst starts during the impulsive phase of the first flare; the second starts near the peak of the third flare and has a larger drift rate. The first burst's radio sources lie along the nose-front of a shock-like EUV wave near 09:06 UT, whereas the second burst's sources lie along the shock flank near 09:55 UT, consistent with the EUV wave structures at the same times.
AI.conclusion: Two coronal shocks from two CMEs can generate multiple type-II radio bursts in a single event. The radio sources trace different parts of the shock (nose vs. flank), demonstrating the value of combined EUV and radio imaging, and highlighting the need for projection and scattering corrections in the second event.

title: The 10 Mpc Volume
comment: Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal. 32 pages, 30 figures
summary: Accurate distances are now known for most unobscured galaxies brighter than MB = -13 mag within 10 Mpc from Hubble Space Telescope observations of their luminous stars. Complementary mid-infrared observations with the Wide-field Infrared Explorer provide global stellar mass estimates for these galaxies. Consequences are detailed knowledge of the properties of the Universe in a volume-limited space. Galaxies tend to lie within groups, within filaments. The filaments experience bulk motions in response to well defined gravitational attractors such as the Virgo Cluster and repulsors such as the Local Void. The groups are inevitably dominated by a single galaxy, with 10 galaxies between one and nine Mpc containing most of the stellar mass within the sample. There is a curious lack of galaxies in an interval fainter than these dominant galaxies. The dominant galaxies in halos tend to have gas reservoirs and ongoing star formation, a property extending to dwarf galaxies in separate halos. Secondary galaxies in halos are frequently gas depleted and lack evidence of star formation. With one notable exception, all galaxies in the complete sample have well formed red giant branches indicative of early-onset star formation.

AI.tldr: A volume-limited census within 10 Mpc yields accurate distances and stellar masses for nearby galaxies, revealing group/filament structure, bulk motions driven by the Virgo Cluster and Local Void, dominant-galaxy hierarchies, and a bimodal star-formation pattern tied to halo role.
AI.motivation: To obtain a detailed, volume-limited understanding of the local Universe's galaxy properties, which requires reliable distances and global stellar masses for a complete sample of nearby galaxies.
AI.method: Combines Hubble Space Telescope observations of luminous stars (tip of the red giant branch distances) for most unobscured galaxies brighter than MB = -13 mag within 10 Mpc with complementary Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer mid-infrared global stellar mass estimates.
AI.result: Galaxies cluster into groups within filaments that undergo bulk motions responding to attractors (Virgo Cluster) and repulsors (Local Void).
